6.2 Fund Costs

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

All lessons, questions and reference answers on this site were generated by AI and have not been reviewed by a professional. Their correctness is not guaranteed. If you find an error, please report it with the link at the bottom of the page. The content is for learning only and is not investment advice.

Expected returns can only be estimated as a range (4.11 Capital Market Assumptions), but costs are almost certain: paying 1% more in fees means earning 1% less, for sure. This lesson sorts fund costs into several kinds and looks at how they affect long-run wealth.

The expense ratio

Section titled “The expense ratio”

The expense ratio is a fund’s yearly operating expenses as a share of its average assets. It includes the management fee paid to the fund’s adviser, administrative costs such as custody, accounting and legal fees, and the 12b-1 fee discussed below. The expense ratio is not billed to investors separately; it is deducted from fund assets every day and shows up in the NAV (net asset value).

US fund fees have fallen sharply over the past thirty years. According to the Investment Company Institute (ICI), the asset-weighted average expense ratio of stock mutual funds fell from 1.04% in 1996 to 0.40% in 2025, and that of stock index ETFs was 0.14%; by the end of 2024, index mutual funds and ETFs held 51% of long-term fund assets. Some broad index funds charge only about 0.03%.

Check C1
A fund reports a return of 8% over the past year, and its expense ratio is 0.6%. An investor who held the fund the whole year earned about 7.4% after the expense ratio.
How is the expense ratio collected? Which price is the reported return computed from?

Sales loads and share classes

Section titled “Sales loads and share classes”

Some funds sold through brokers also charge sales loads, which pay the brokers’ commissions:

  • A front-end load is deducted at purchase: with 10,000 dollars invested and a 5.75% front-end load, only 9,425 dollars is actually invested. When a single purchase reaches certain amounts (breakpoints), the rate falls.
  • A back-end load (or CDSC) is charged on sales within a certain number of years and declines year by year.
  • A 12b-1 fee is a yearly marketing and service fee taken from fund assets under SEC Rule 12b-1, included in the expense ratio. Under FINRA rules it is at most 1% a year.

The share classes of one fund charge these fees in different ways: Class A charges a front-end load and a lower 12b-1 fee; Class C charges no front-end load but a higher 12b-1 fee, and usually converts to Class A automatically after a number of years; share classes for institutions or adviser platforms usually charge neither. Funds without sales loads are called no-load funds. ICI data show that in 2025 about 92% of the money flowing into long-term mutual funds went to share classes with neither a sales load nor a 12b-1 fee.

Check C2
A broker recommends to a client a large-cap fund with a 5.75% front-end load rather than a no-load index fund with a similar strategy and a lower expense ratio. The most likely reason is:
Who receives the load? Does it pay the fund's managers or the sales channel?
The question says this fund's expense ratio is higher than the index fund's. Does the front-end load change its future yearly expense ratio?

Trading costs and cash drag

Section titled “Trading costs and cash drag”

The expense ratio does not include the cost of the fund’s own trading: commissions, bid–ask spreads (bid-ask spread) and the market impact of large trades. These costs lower the fund’s return directly but do not appear in the fee table. The measure of how much a fund trades is the turnover ratio: the amount bought or sold in a year (whichever is smaller) as a share of average assets. A turnover of 100% roughly means the fund replaced its whole portfolio once in the year.

Funds usually hold some cash to meet redemptions. When stocks are expected to earn more than cash, this cash makes the fund’s return lower than if it were fully invested in stocks; this is called cash drag. On the other hand, index funds can lend their stocks to short sellers and earn securities lending income, offsetting part of their costs.

Check C3
Two active stock funds both have an expense ratio of 0.75%; one has a turnover of 20% and the other 150%. Since the expense ratios are equal, the two funds' total yearly costs are about the same.
Are the commissions, spreads and market impact a fund pays when trading included in its expense ratio? How do these costs change as turnover rises?

Tracking difference and tracking error

Section titled “Tracking difference and tracking error”

For an index fund, all costs end up in the gap between its return and the index’s. The average of the fund’s return minus the index return is the tracking difference; it measures how much the fund lags (or leads) the index per year on average. The standard deviation of this gap is the tracking error (tracking error); it measures how unsteady the gap is. The expense ratio, trading costs and cash drag make the tracking difference negative, and securities lending income moves it toward positive.

Check C4
An index fund's tracking error is very small, close to 0. From this one can conclude that its yearly return is almost equal to the index's.
Tracking error is the standard deviation of what? If a fund lagged the index by a steady 1% every year, what would its tracking error be?

How fees compound

Section titled “How fees compound”

Fees are deducted from assets every year, and the future returns on the money taken are lost as well, so the effect of fees on final wealth builds up over time (Exercises Question 1).

Check C5
In Figure 5-1, keep the fee at 1% and raise the return before fees from 2% to 10%. What happens to the share of final wealth lost after 30 years?
With higher returns fees do take more dollars, but final wealth is larger too. Look at the readout in the figure: how much does the share change?
The 1% fee is indeed a smaller share of the return, but it is the same share of assets. Which of these does the share of final wealth lost depend on?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • The expense ratio is deducted from fund assets every day and shows up in the NAV; the average expense ratio of US stock funds has fallen sharply.
  • Sales loads (front-end and back-end) and 12b-1 fees pay the sales channel; the share classes of one fund charge in different ways.
  • Trading costs (commissions, spreads, market impact) rise with turnover and are not included in the expense ratio; holding cash causes cash drag.
  • Tracking difference measures how much an index fund lags its index on average; tracking error measures how much the gap varies.
  • The effect of fees on final wealth compounds over time.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
A 30-year-old investor plans to hold a stock fund for 35 years. The fund's return before fees is 6.5% a year.
(a) Write the share of final wealth lost after 35 years, compared with no fee, in terms of the expense ratio fff, the return rrr and the number of years TTT, and explain why it is close to 1−e−fT1 - e^{-fT}1−e−fT. Compute the share lost with expense ratios of 0.8% and 0.04%.
(b) A salesperson says: "This fund charges only 0.8% a year, 80 cents per 100 dollars, which hardly affects your returns." Evaluate this statement.
Question 2
A fund has two share classes: Class A has a 5.75% front-end load and an expense ratio of 0.85%; Class C has no front-end load and an expense ratio of 1.60% (including a 1% 12b-1 fee), and converts automatically to Class A after 8 years (with no load at conversion). The fund returns 7% a year before the expense ratio, and the expense ratio is deducted yearly (the yearly return is 7%7\%7% minus the expense ratio).
(a) If Class C never converted, after how many years would Class A be better?
(b) Taking the conversion into account, which class ends with more wealth after 20 years, and by how many percent? A broker says: "For long-term investors, Class A is always the better deal." Evaluate this statement, and say what question matters more for this investor.
Question 3
An active stock fund has an expense ratio of 0.70% and a turnover of 80%, and its trading cost (spread and market impact) is estimated at 0.4% of the amount traded per round trip. It holds 5% cash on average, earning 4%, while stocks are expected to return 8%.
(a) Estimate the fund's yearly trading cost, cash drag and total cost.
(b) The fund's marketing says: "Our total fees are only 0.70%, very competitive with similar funds." Evaluate this statement. In which public documents can an investor find the information needed to estimate these costs?
Question 4
Two ETFs track the S&P 500. X has an expense ratio of 0.03%, an average tracking difference of −0.05% over the past 10 years and a bid–ask spread of 0.01%. Y has an expense ratio of 0.09%, an average tracking difference of −0.04% (more securities lending income) and a bid–ask spread of 0.03%. The spread cost of one round trip is about one bid–ask spread.
(a) For an investor who buys and holds for 20 years, roughly what is the yearly cost of each ETF? And for an investor who makes one round trip every month?
(b) A friend says: "Index funds are all the same; just pick the lowest expense ratio." Evaluate this statement.
